title: E-Business Security, Privacy and Legal Issues
part: Part B — Cyber Safety and E-Commerce

blocks.html: After studying this chapter you will be able to:

items.html: name the main security threats to e-business
explain the goals of information security: confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication and non-repudiation
describe encryption, HTTPS, digital certificates, firewalls and multi-factor authentication
explain privacy, cookies and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
describe legal and ethical issues in e-business, including e-contracts, intellectual property, taxation and consumer protection

blocks.html: An online shop stores customers' names, addresses, phone numbers and payment details. If criminals steal this data, customers lose money and trust, and the company faces losses, legal penalties and a damaged reputation. Security, privacy and legal compliance are therefore as important to an e-business as a lock is to a shop.

rows: Criminals break into servers and steal customer databases
Malicious software steals data or locks company systems
Fake websites and messages using the company's name
Website flooded so that customers cannot place orders
Data intercepted between the customer and the website, especially on unsafe public Wi-Fi
Stolen cards used to buy goods; fake refund claims
Weak website code exploited to read or change the database (e.g. SQL injection)
Damage customers and the platform's reputation

blocks.html: The three main goals are called the CIA triad:

rows: Only authorised people can read the data
Your card number is hidden from other customers and staff
Data is not changed without permission
An order of ₹500 cannot be altered to ₹5000 on the way
Systems work whenever they are needed
The ticket-booking site stays up during busy hours

blocks.html: Two more goals matter in e-commerce:

items.html: Authentication — proving that a user or website is who it claims to be (passwords, OTP, certificates).
Non-repudiation — a person cannot later deny an action they performed, such as placing an order or signing a contract (digital signatures, transaction logs).

blocks.html: Encryption converts readable data (plaintext) into a scrambled form (ciphertext) using a key. Only someone with the correct key can decrypt it back.

blocks.caption: Figure 8.1 · How encryption protects an online payment

rows: The same secret key encrypts and decrypts
A public key encrypts; only the matching private key decrypts
Fast; good for large amounts of data
Slower; solves the problem of sharing keys safely
Public key can be given to anyone

blocks.html: In practice, HTTPS uses public-key encryption to agree on a secret key, then fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the session.

TLS (Transport Layer Security), the successor of SSL, encrypts data between your browser and a website. A site using it shows https:// and a padlock. Never enter passwords or payment details on a site without HTTPS.

A digital certificate is an electronic ID card for a website, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). It proves that the website really belongs to the company it claims to be, so attackers cannot easily impersonate it. Clicking the padlock shows the certificate details.
A digital signature proves who signed a document and that it was not changed (integrity and non-repudiation). It is legally valid in India under the IT Act, 2000.

items.html: Something you know — password, PIN.
Something you have — phone receiving an OTP, a security key.
Something you are — fingerprint, face.
Two-factor / multi-factor authentication (2FA/MFA) combines two or more of these.
CAPTCHA checks that a user is a human, not a bot.
Firewall — hardware or software that filters network traffic and blocks unauthorised access.
Antivirus and anti-malware on all systems.
Access control — each employee can see only the data needed for their job.
Regular updates and patches to fix security holes.
Backups stored separately, to recover from ransomware or disasters.
Security audits and penetration testing by ethical hackers.
Card security standards (PCI DSS) for anyone handling card data.
Card tokenisation — since October 2022, RBI rules require that merchants do not store full card numbers; a token is stored instead.
Fraud detection — software that flags unusual transactions.

blocks.html: Privacy is a person's right to control how their personal information is collected, used and shared. E-businesses collect a lot of personal data: name, address, phone, email, location, purchase history, browsing behaviour and payment details.

A cookie is a small text file a website stores in your browser to remember you — for example, keeping you logged in or remembering your cart. Third-party cookies placed by advertisers track you across websites to show targeted ads. Browsers let you view, block or delete cookies.

A privacy policy is a statement on a website that explains what data is collected, why, how long it is kept, with whom it is shared and how users can contact the company. Users should read it, at least briefly, before giving personal data.
India's DPDP Act, 2023 protects digital personal data.

items.html: The person whose data it is is the Data Principal; the organisation that decides how to use it is the Data Fiduciary.
Data may be processed only for a lawful purpose with the person's consent (with some exceptions), and only as much as needed.
Data Principals have the right to access information about their data, correct and erase it, and to grievance redressal.
Organisations must keep data secure and report breaches.
Children's data needs verifiable parental consent; tracking and targeted advertising aimed at children is not allowed.
A Data Protection Board of India can impose penalties of up to ₹250 crore for serious failures.
Share only what is necessary; leave optional fields blank.
Check app permissions (location, contacts, camera).
Use private browsing on shared computers and log out after use.
Clear cookies regularly and decline unnecessary tracking.

rows: Under the IT Act, 2000, contracts made electronically (e.g. clicking "I agree") are legally valid
Legally equal to handwritten signatures (IT Act)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and E-Commerce Rules, 2020: clear prices, return policies, grievance officer, no fake reviews (Chapter 7)
Selling fake branded goods violates trademark; copying product photos or descriptions violates copyright
Registering a domain similar to a famous brand to sell it or mislead people is cybersquatting; disputes can be settled through domain dispute procedures and courts
Online sales attract GST; e-commerce operators must collect tax at source (TCS) on sellers' sales
DPDP Act, 2023 and IT Act sections 43A and 72A on protecting data
Fraud, hacking, identity theft punished under the IT Act and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Chapter 6)
When buyer, seller and server are in different places or countries, deciding which court hears a case can be complex

items.html: Honest product descriptions and genuine reviews.
Not exploiting customers' data or addiction to apps.
Fair treatment of delivery workers and small sellers.
Not using "dark patterns" — tricky designs that push people into purchases or subscriptions they did not intend.

blocks.html: Did you know? The CIA triad has nothing to do with the American intelligence agency — the letters stand for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, the three pillars of information security.

lessons.title: Workshop 8: Check the security and privacy of websites

blocks.html: Aim: To examine security and privacy features of real websites.

items.html: Inspect HTTPS. Open three shopping or banking websites. Click the padlock and note who the certificate is issued to and by whom.
Find the privacy policy. For one website, find the privacy policy and note: what data is collected, why, with whom it is shared and how to contact the grievance officer.
Cookies. In your browser settings, view the cookies stored by one website. Then clear cookies and notice what changes (e.g. you are logged out).
App permissions. On a phone, review the permissions of five apps. Turn off any permission an app does not need.

Encryption by hand. Use a simple Caesar cipher (shift each letter by 3: A→D, B→E …) to encrypt PATNA. Exchange encrypted words with a partner and decrypt them. (Answer: SDWQD.) Discuss why real encryption needs much stronger methods.
E-businesses face threats such as data breaches, malware, phishing, DoS attacks, man-in-the-middle attacks, payment fraud and insider misuse.
Security goals: confidentiality, integrity, availability (CIA), plus authentication and non-repudiation.
Encryption (symmetric and asymmetric), TLS/HTTPS, digital certificates, digital signatures, MFA, firewalls, backups, audits and card tokenisation protect e-business.
Privacy is the right to control personal data; cookies, privacy policies and app permissions affect it; the DPDP Act, 2023 gives people rights over their data.
Legal issues include e-contracts, digital signatures, consumer protection, intellectual property, cybersquatting, GST and jurisdiction; ethics forbid fake reviews and dark patterns.
